newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Sweden to survive any EMU backlash.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Sweden to survive any EMU backlash.

text.p: Swedish bonds are vulnerable to a knee-jerk setback if lingering hopes of early EMU membership are dashed by the government this week, economists said on Wednesday.
But any decision by Sweden not to throw its hat into the single currency ring from the outset will have been so well sign-posted that negative fall-out would be limited, they added.
"Nothing's ever really completely factored in, and doubtless (a decision on EMU) would move the market," said Julian Jessop, European economist at Nikko Securities in London.
"But not a lot -- it might be worth a few basis points on the spread."
A report on Swedish radio on Wednesday said the Swedish government would not join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) during the mandate period 1998-2002 without new parliamentary elections.
It said this meant either new elections must be held or Sweden would have to wait until 2003 to join the single currency, following scheduled parliamentary elections in 2002.

A spokeswoman for Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson declined to comment on the radio report, saying the ruling Social Democrats would announce their view shortly on membership of EMU. The radio report said this announcement would be made on Friday.

James McKay, an economist at PaineWebber, agreed most of the negative reaction had already been priced in to the market. He noted the Swedish/German 10-year bond spread had snapped out six basis points to 118 on Wednesday morning from the prior close.
"There was some speculation that we could see entry for Sweden in 2001, so perhaps the market will be a touch disappointed," he said.
"We could see a snap negative reaction, but that will be limited to around 125 basis points on the spread."
But McKay said he expected Swedish debt to remain broadly positive in the next month or so with the spread heading back down to around 100 basis points, ahead of widening again later in the year.
"I would use any negative sentiment over the details of EMU intentions as a buying opportunity (for Sweden) short term," said McKay.
"But you should be very cautious because these high-yielding markets are potential time-bombs later in the year."
Stephanie Pfeifer, European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the degree of negative fall-out for Swedish debt depended on the wording of any government statement on its EMU intentions.
"Obviously, the more positively phrased the better. But if there is anything in the statement that hints at a new election or a referendum...that would be negative."

Economists said any investment allocation decisions within the Nordic block should be made in the broader context of what a unified Europe would look like, should the left-wing win the French election on Sunday.
They said that was currently dictating sentiment on the likely strength and breadth of monetary union, with implications for relative debt market performances in the Nordic economies.
If convergence trades stay on track in the shorter term, investors in the Nordic block would do well to keep their money in Finland, said Jessop.
Finland is a member of the EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), viewed as a step towards joining EMU in the first round.
But if, longer term, the prospect of a soft or delayed euro gathers pace, Denmark will appeal.

"Denmark clearly offers the best safe-haven potential," said McKay. "It's opt-out of EMU limits the potential for EMU problems to feed through to Denmark...I would expect some spread widening later in the year, but that opt-out does limit it."
